title: The barber-surgeons

confidence.note: The 1540 Act of Parliament and the company it created are documented in the company's own records and later histories; the 1745 separation is equally well recorded. The only shaky part of the popular story is its medieval back-story, covered below.

people: Thomas Vicary, surgeon to Henry VIII
summary: In 1540 Henry VIII's Parliament joined London's barbers and surgeons into one company, which got four hanged felons a year to dissect.
body: Surgery was long a craft learned by apprenticeship. London's barbers did more than shave: they bled patients, cupped, pulled teeth and lanced abscesses, while a smaller guild of surgeons competed with them for work. In 1540, urged on by Thomas Vicary, surgeon to Henry VIII, Parliament merged the two into the Company of Barber-Surgeons; Holbein painted the king handing over the Act. The company was also given the bodies of four executed criminals a year for public anatomy lessons. The uneasy partnership lasted until 1745, when the surgeons left to form the company that became the Royal College of Surgeons.

myth.tradition: The Church banned surgery at the Council of Tours in 1163 ('the Church abhors blood'), so the work fell to barbers.
myth.record: The Tours canon only stopped monks and regular canons from leaving their houses to study medicine or secular law. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council barred subdeacons, deacons and priests from surgery involving cutting or burning; lay surgeons were unaffected.

title: Medicine in print

confidence.note: Both editions carry printed dates and survive in many copies. Calling the *Fasciculus* the first printed book with anatomical illustrations is the standard judgment of librarians, though it depends on how 'anatomical' is defined.

people: Nicolaus Laurentii, Florentine printer of Celsus
Johannes and Gregorius de Gregoriis, Venetian printers
Johannes de Ketham (fl. 1460), physician whose name the *Fasciculus* carries
summary: Within decades of Gutenberg, medicine went to press: Celsus in 1478, then a Venetian anthology whose woodcuts were the first printed anatomical pictures.
body: In 1478, about a quarter of a century after the first printed books, the Florentine printer Nicolaus Laurentii issued the first printed edition of the Roman writer Celsus's *De medicina*. In 1491 the Gregorii brothers of Venice printed the *Fasciculus medicinae*, a bundle of short medical treatises, many of them medieval, including advice on avoiding plague. Its woodcuts, including a zodiac man and a dissection scene, made it the first printed book with anatomical illustrations. It ran through fourteen editions and translations in 24 years. Its nominal author, Johannes de Ketham, may only have owned the manuscript.

title: The great pox

confidence.note: Contemporary writers agree that the epidemic broke out among the armies fighting over Naples in 1494–95. Where it came from is still argued: ancient DNA now favors an American origin, but specialists disagree over possible pre-1492 cases in European skeletons.

place: Naples, Italy, then all of Europe
people: Charles VIII, king of France, whose army spread the disease
Girolamo Fracastoro (c. 1478–1553), physician-poet who named it
summary: In 1495 a new and ghastly disease burst out of a French army in Italy. Europe blamed its neighbors; scientists still argue over where it came from.
body: In 1494 Charles VIII of France marched an army recruited across Western Europe down Italy to claim Naples. In its camps a disfiguring illness unknown to physicians broke out, and when the soldiers went home in 1495 they took it with them; within five years it had spread throughout Europe. Witnesses described boils 'that stood out like acorns', a sickening stench and terrible pain. Everyone blamed someone else: the French called it the Neapolitan disease, the English and Italians the French disease. The name we use comes from a Latin poem of 1530 by Girolamo Fracastoro, in which a shepherd called Syphilus is struck down by Apollo. Doctors treated it with mercury and with guaiacum, a wood from the Americas.

Because the outbreak followed so soon after Columbus returned in 1493, people suspected early on that it came from the New World. The question is still open. Claimed pre-Columbian cases in European skeletons are hard to tell apart from related infections such as yaws, or are poorly dated. Ancient bacterial genomes from the Americas, published in 2024, point to an American origin for the whole family of syphilis bacteria, though their authors warn against dismissing the European evidence.

title: Paracelsus burns the books

confidence.note: His appointment at Basel in March 1527 and his flight in February 1528 are documented; the St John's Day burning is reported consistently, though accounts differ on which books went into the fire. His lasting influence is a matter of broad agreement among historians.

people: Paracelsus (Theophrastus von Hohenheim, 1493/94–1541), physician and alchemist
Johannes Froben (d. 1527), Basel publisher and patron
summary: Hired as Basel's city physician in 1527, Paracelsus lectured in German, raged at the apothecaries and threw Avicenna's Canon onto a bonfire.
body: Theophrastus von Hohenheim, who called himself Paracelsus, won the post of city physician and professor at Basel in March 1527 after treating the great publisher Johannes Froben. He lectured in German rather than Latin, admitted barber-surgeons to his classes and attacked the apothecaries' profits. On St John's Day, 24 June, he threw a copy of Avicenna's *Canon*, the standard medical textbook, onto a students' bonfire. When Froben died in October his enemies closed in, and in February 1528 he fled the city, to wander for the rest of his life.

His medicine mixed alchemy, astrology and sharp observation. He rejected the theory of the four humors, sought chemical causes and chemical cures for disease, wrote the first book on the diseases of miners, and condemned guaiacum for syphilis in favor of mercury. Few of his works were printed in his lifetime; after his death in 1541 they appeared by the hundreds and inspired a school of chemical medicine.

myth.tradition: Paracelsus publicly burned the collected works of Galen and Avicenna, the two pillars of medical authority.
myth.record: Versions differ. The standard scholarly biography says he burned a copy of Avicenna's *Canon* at a student celebration; Galen's books appear only in some retellings.

title: Vesalius, De Humani Corporis Fabrica

confidence.note: The book survives in many copies of the 1543 Basel edition, and its contents can be checked page by page. Historians agree on its importance; they debate who drew the pictures and how quickly its anatomy displaced Galen's.

people: Jan Stephan van Calcar (1499–c. 1546), artist sometimes credited with the woodcuts
summary: A 28-year-old professor at Padua published the most famous anatomy book ever printed, built on human dissection and dazzling woodcuts.
body: In 1543 Andreas Vesalius, a 28-year-old professor of surgery and anatomy at Padua, published *De humani corporis fabrica*, 'seven books on the fabric of the human body'. He had it printed across the Alps in Basel by Joannes Oporinus, alongside a short *Epitome* for students. Its woodcuts became instantly famous: a title page showing Vesalius dissecting a corpse amid a jostling crowd, skeletons and flayed 'muscle men' posed like classical statues against the countryside around Padua, even decorated capital letters showing cherubs robbing graves.

Medical teaching then rested on the ancient authority of Galen. Vesalius had come to see that Galen's anatomy came largely from animals. In public demonstrations at Bologna in 1540 he declared that human anatomy could be learned only by dissecting human bodies, and he did the cutting himself. The *Fabrica* pointed out where Galen had described apes rather than people: the human jaw is one bone, not two, and the breastbone has three segments, not seven. He also doubted that blood seeped through invisible pores in the wall between the heart's ventricles.

The change was neither instant nor total. The Paris anatomist Jacobus Sylvius, his former teacher, attacked him violently, and Vesalian anatomy gained general support only around 1600, spread by his successors at Padua. Its pictures spread faster, copied and plagiarized across Europe within two years. Vesalius himself soon left research to become physician to Emperor Charles V, though he produced a revised edition in 1555.

Even the details are less tidy than legend. The colophon gives June 1543, but the book actually appeared in August. The artists are unknown: Jan Stephan van Calcar was long credited, but most scholars now point to several hands from Titian's workshop in Venice.

myth.tradition: With the *Fabrica*, Vesalius swept away Galen's anatomy at a stroke.
myth.record: Vesalius relied heavily on Galen, sometimes translating him word for word, and kept Galen's idea that blood is made in the liver. His corrections met fierce opposition and were broadly accepted only about two generations later.

links.note: Corrected many points of Galen's animal-based anatomy.

title: Ambroise Paré and gentler surgery

confidence.note: Paré's 1545 book on gunshot wounds is a dated publication. The famous night at Turin is known only from his own account written decades later, and sources place it in 1536 or 1537.

people: Ambroise Paré (c. 1510–1590), military and royal surgeon
summary: A barber-surgeon who ran out of boiling oil on campaign found his patients did better without it, and spent his life making surgery less brutal.
body: Ambroise Paré trained not at a university but as a barber-surgeon's apprentice and a surgical dresser at the Hôtel-Dieu in Paris. Gunshot wounds were then thought to be poisoned by gunpowder and were seared with boiling oil. Serving with the French army at Turin, Paré ran out of oil and improvised a dressing of egg yolk, oil of roses and turpentine. Next day, he wrote, the men he had dressed were free from pain, their wounds neither inflamed nor swollen, unlike those treated with oil. His book on gunshot wounds of 1545, written in French because he knew no Latin, made him famous.

He went on to revive the ancient practice of tying off blood vessels during amputation instead of burning them shut, designed instruments and artificial limbs, and served four kings of France. He ended case histories with a modest formula: 'I dressed him, God healed him.' The Turin story comes from his own account published almost half a century later.

myth.record: The story is old and still repeated, but the evidence shows he remained a Roman Catholic throughout his life.

title: Fracastoro's seeds of contagion

confidence.note: *De contagione* was printed in Venice in 1546 and its contents are not in doubt. How far his 'seeds' anticipate microbes is a matter of interpretation, and historians are more cautious than older admirers.

summary: Three centuries before Pasteur, a Veronese poet-physician argued that diseases spread by tiny seeds passed by touch, clothing and the air.
body: In 1546 Girolamo Fracastoro, the Veronese physician who had named syphilis in verse, published *De contagione*. He argued that contagious diseases spread through tiny 'seeds' (*seminaria*) in three ways: by direct contact, as in scabies; by 'fomites' such as clothes and sheets; and at a distance, as with plague and smallpox. He gave an early description of typhus and discussed the contagiousness of tuberculosis, measles and rabies. His seeds owed much to the ancient atomism of Lucretius, and the rival idea that bad air caused epidemics stayed dominant for three more centuries.

myth.tradition: Fracastoro discovered the germ theory of disease three centuries before Pasteur.
myth.record: His *seminaria* had some lifelike traits, but they came from ancient philosophy, not observation; whether he foresaw microbes cannot be established, and his ideas were largely overshadowed.

links.note: The new pox shaped his thinking about contagion.
The germ theory his seeds are often said to foreshadow.

title: The Chamberlens' secret forceps

confidence.note: The family kept no public record of the invention, so its date is inferred: the Science Museum credits Peter Chamberlen the Elder (d. 1631), while another library account dates a practical design to the 1640s. That the secret was kept for about a century is well attested.

people: Peter Chamberlen the Elder (d. 1631), barber-surgeon and man-midwife
Hugh Chamberlen the Elder (c. 1630–c. 1720), obstetrician who may have sold the secret
summary: For over a century one family of London man-midwives guarded a simple instrument that could save mothers and babies in obstructed labor.
body: The Chamberlens, French Protestants who settled in England in 1569, became a dynasty of man-midwives famous for handling difficult births. Their secret was a short forceps whose two blades, inserted one at a time and then joined, could grip a baby's head. Peter Chamberlen the Elder (d. 1631), who attended the queens of James I and Charles I, is thought to have devised it. The family kept the design to itself for over a hundred years. Hugh Chamberlen may have sold it to a Dutch obstetrician in 1692; forceps were common knowledge by the 1730s.

title: Santorio weighs himself

confidence.note: *De statica medicina* is dated 1614 and Santorio's instruments are described in his own printed works; the exact date he added a scale to the thermoscope is unknown, sometime between 1602 and 1612.

people: Santorio Santorio (1561–1636), physician and professor at Padua
summary: A Padua professor sat for years on a weighing chair to measure what the body loses invisibly, and helped turn the thermoscope into a thermometer.
body: Santorio Santorio, professor of theoretical medicine at Padua from 1611, sat in a chair hung from a balance and weighed himself, his food and his excreta, reportedly over some thirty years. The difference revealed 'insensible perspiration', moisture lost unseen through skin and lungs, which he found exceeded all visible excretions combined. His little book of aphorisms, *De statica medicina* (1614), went through dozens of editions. A friend of Galileo, he also added a scale to the thermoscope, making a thermometer, and timed pulses with a pendulum. He still worked within humoral medicine, but insisted on measuring it.

links.note: Padua's new experimental physiology a generation later.
Santorio's thermometer was the remote ancestor of the clinical thermometer.
